blocks.title: Osmoregulation
blocks.text: Osmoregulation is the process by which an organism maintains a stable internal equilibrium of water and dissolved substances, irrespective of the surrounding environmental conditions.

Many marine organisms undergo osmosis without any regulatory system, because their cells have the same osmotic pressure as the sea. Other organisms must actively acquire, retain or eliminate water or salts to regulate their internal water and mineral balance.

items: A hypotonic solution has a lower solute concentration than the inside of the cell, so water enters the cell by osmosis and it swells.
A hypertonic solution has a higher solute concentration than the inside of the cell, so water moves out and the cell shrinks; in a plant cell this loss of water is plasmolysis.
An isotonic solution has a solute concentration like that inside the cell, so there is no net movement of water between the cell and its environment.

blocks.alt: Three plant cells. In the hypotonic solution blue arrows point inward and the membrane presses tight against the wall. In the isotonic solution arrows point both ways and the cell keeps its shape. In the hypertonic solution arrows point outward and the membrane and contents have shrunk away from the wall.
blocks.caption: A plant cell in hypotonic, isotonic and hypertonic solutions (original diagram after Figure 8.16).
blocks.long_description: In a hypotonic solution water enters by osmosis, the cell swells and becomes turgid, and the wall stops it bursting. In an isotonic solution there is no net water movement and the cell keeps its shape. In a hypertonic solution water leaves, the protoplast shrinks away from the wall and the cell is plasmolysed.

blocks.text: Plants live in aquatic, moderate, severely dry and saline habitats and are called hydrophytes, mesophytes, xerophytes and halophytes respectively.

Hydrophytes are adapted to aquatic environments, marine and freshwater, by specialised osmotic adjustments. Marine hydrophytes live in saline (hypertonic) conditions where water tends to leave their cells; they excrete excess salt through salt glands, synthesise organic solutes such as proline, glycine betaine and sugars to retain water by raising their internal osmotic potential, have thick cuticles that reduce water loss, and show halophytic traits that tolerate high salinity. Freshwater hydrophytes live in hypotonic surroundings where water continuously enters their cells; they expel excess water through structures such as hydathodes or vacuoles, actively absorb essential ions such as potassium and calcium to keep osmotic balance in dilute surroundings, have thin or absent cuticles that ease water exchange, and often have reduced root systems, absorbing nutrients and water directly from the water. Examples are water lilies, lotus, seaweeds and tape grass.

Mesophytes live in moderate environments that are neither too dry nor too wet, preferring soil that is not waterlogged and has moderate salt and humidity. They have well-developed roots and shoots with a fully formed vascular system and need no special adaptations. Their leaves are flat, broad and green with stomata on the surface. Examples are rose, tomato and daisy.

Xerophytes are adapted to survive dry conditions, with special adaptations to minimise water loss and store water. Plants that store water are succulents, with fleshy stems that hold water for use when needed. Other adaptations include waxy coatings on the leaves to reduce water loss, leaf drop in dry periods, and leaf folding or repositioning to absorb sunlight efficiently. Examples are thorn trees, desert marigold and blue agave.

Halophytes inhabit saline soil with high concentrations of salts such as NaCl, MgCl2 and MgSO4, or saline water; only plants that tolerate such salt concentrations can grow there. They have succulent leaves and sometimes succulent stems, and in some the leaves are modified into spines. Examples are sea arrowgrass and sea lavender.

blocks.title: Mangroves
blocks.text: Halophytes growing in marshy places near the seashore form a special vegetation known as mangrove or tidal woodland; they are also called helophilous halophytes.

blocks.prompt: A freshwater plant and a seaweed each face a constant osmotic problem. State the problem and one adjustment for each.
blocks.explanation: The freshwater plant sits in hypotonic water, so water keeps entering its cells; it expels the excess through hydathodes or vacuoles and actively absorbs ions to keep its balance. The seaweed sits in hypertonic seawater, so water tends to leave; it excretes excess salt through salt glands and makes organic solutes such as proline to hold water.

items: Osmoregulation keeps internal water and solutes steady. Hypotonic surroundings swell a cell, hypertonic shrink it (plasmolysis in plants), isotonic leave it unchanged.

Hydrophytes: marine ones excrete salt, make organic solutes and have thick cuticles; freshwater ones expel water, absorb ions, have thin cuticles and small roots. Mesophytes need no special adaptation. Xerophytes store water in succulent stems and cut loss with wax, leaf drop and folding. Halophytes tolerate salt with succulent leaves and stems; mangroves are shore halophytes.
